title: Structure of algebraic normalized DVR base changes
statement: Let $A\to B$ be an injective local map of discrete valuation rings [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring], with fraction fields $K\subseteq L$. For an algebraic field extension $P/K$ [def-pc-field-extension], let $R_P$ be the integral closure of $A$ in $P$ and $C_P$ the integral closure of $B$ in $E_P=(L\otimes_KP)_{\mathrm{red}}$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure, def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. The reduction is the quotient by all nilpotents. Suppose either (a) $P/K$ is finite, or (b) $B$ is essentially of finite type over $A$ and $R_P$ is Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring]. Essentially of finite type means $B\cong U_{\mathfrak p}$ as $A$-algebras for a finitely generated $A$-algebra $U$ [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra] and prime $\mathfrak p$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. Then $E_P$ is a nonempty finite product of fields algebraic over $L$; $R_P$ and $C_P$ are Noetherian with finitely many maximal ideals; $R_P$ is a domain and $C_P$ is a finite product of integrally closed domains of dimension one. For every maximal ideal $q$ of $C_P$, its contraction $n=q\cap R_P$ is maximal, both $(R_P)_n$ and $(C_P)_q$ are discrete valuation rings, and the residue field extension $\kappa(q)/\kappa(n)$ is finitely generated in case (b). Every maximal ideal of $R_P$ is the contraction of a maximal ideal of $C_P$. In case (a), $\kappa(n)/(A/\mathfrak m_A)$ and $\kappa(q)/(B/\mathfrak m_B)$ are finite field extensions. Here dimension one means that every nonzero prime in each domain factor is maximal and at least one such prime exists; integrally closed means containing every element of its fraction field integral over it. Local maps are those pulling back maximal ideals to maximal ideals. Neither case requires separability.

source.place: Tag 09IH, lemma-big-extension-is-ok, statement and proof; Tag 09EM, remark-construction, finite base extensions, assertions (1)–(4); the finite residue-field assertion is the cited algebra-lemma-finite-extension-residue-fields-dimension-1.

proof.text: Write $R=R_P$, $C=C_P$, $E=E_P$ and choose a uniformizer $\pi$ of $A$. The algebraic integral-closure theorem gives $A\subset R\subset P$, $\operatorname{Frac}(R)=P$, and normality of $R$. In case (a), the finite-extension Dedekind theorem makes $R$ Noetherian of dimension one; in case (b), Noetherianity is assumed and integral dimension invariance gives dimension one. All maximal ideals of $R$ contract to $\mathfrak m_A$, so all contain $\pi$. Every prime containing $\pi$ is maximal by integrality over $A$. They are consequently all minimal over $(\pi)$, and are finite in number by the finite-minimal-primes theorem. Thus $R$ is a semilocal normal Noetherian domain of dimension one in both cases.

The $A$-modules $B$ and $R$ are torsion free, hence flat over the PID $A$. Since $A\to B$ is local it is faithfully flat. Put $D=B\otimes_A R$. Base change makes $R\to D$ faithfully flat, and makes $B\to D$ integral. Flatness of $R$ preserves the injection $A\hookrightarrow B$, so $R\hookrightarrow D$; flatness of $B$ similarly gives $B\hookrightarrow D$. Tensoring multiplication by $\pi$ on $R$ with the flat module $B$ shows that $\pi$ is a nonzerodivisor of $D$. The image of $\pi$ in $B$ is a positive power of a uniformizer times a unit, since the map of DVRs is injective and local.

source.place: Tag 09EM, remark-construction (2), flatness justification expanded; Tag 09IH, proof

proof.text: We have $R[1/\pi]=P$: for $x\in P$, multiply a polynomial equation over $K$ by a sufficiently large power of $\pi$ after replacing $x$ by $\pi^N x$, to obtain a monic equation for $\pi^N x$ over $A$. Hence $\pi^N x\in R$. The localization-tensor theorem now identifies $D[1/\pi]$ with $L\otimes_K P$, because $B[1/\pi]=L$. On pure fractions the identification is $(b\otimes r)/\pi^j\mapsto (b/\pi^j)\otimes r$, and its inverse is obtained by putting the finitely many denominators into one power of $\pi$. Reduction commutes with this localization: $d/\pi^j$ is nilpotent exactly when $\pi^k d^h=0$ for some $k,h$, which, by regularity of $\pi$, means $d$ is nilpotent. Thus, for $G=D_{\mathrm{red}}$, $E=G[1/\pi]$ and $G\hookrightarrow E$.

The algebra $L\otimes_KP$ is nonzero, since field-extension base change is faithfully flat and therefore injective. Its reduction is nonzero too (otherwise $1$ would be nilpotent). Since an algebraic field extension is integral, integral base change makes $L\to L\otimes_KP$, and hence $L\to E$, integral. Every prime of $E$ is maximal, being over the unique prime of the field $L$. In particular, all its residue fields are algebraic over $L$: a monic equation for an element descends to the quotient field $E/\mathfrak q$.

source.place: Tags 09EM and 09IH, the generic reduced algebra

proof.text: In case (a), choosing a finite $K$-basis of $P$ shows that $L\otimes_KP$, and therefore $E$, is finite-dimensional over $L$. Thus $E$ is Artinian, and its reduced Artinian decomposition gives $E=\prod_{i=1}^t F_i$ with $t\ge1$ and each $F_i/L$ finite. The integral closure $C_i$ of $B$ in $F_i$ is a Dedekind domain by the finite-extension Dedekind theorem. That theorem gives finite fibres of $\operatorname{Spec}(C_i)\to\operatorname{Spec}(B)$; maximal ideals contract to the unique maximal ideal of $B$, so $C_i$ is semilocal. Integrality is coordinatewise for a finite product: one implication projects a monic equation; for the converse the product of the finitely many monic equations annihilates the tuple. Hence $C=\prod_i C_i$, a Noetherian semilocal product of normal domains of dimension one.

For case (b), choose $B=U_{\mathfrak p}$ with $U$ a finite type $A$-algebra. Then $D$ is the localization of the finite type $R$-algebra $U\otimes_A R$ at the image of $U\setminus\mathfrak p$. The finite-type and localization permanence theorems show $D$ is Noetherian. Integral dimension invariance for $B\hookrightarrow D$ gives $\dim D=1$. Every maximal ideal of $D$ contracts to $\mathfrak m_B$ and contains $\pi$; conversely every prime containing $\pi$ contracts to $\mathfrak m_B$ and is maximal. Thus these primes are precisely the minimal primes over $(\pi)$ and there are finitely many. So $D$ is semilocal. Quotients $G$ and $D/\mathfrak a$ are Noetherian too: they are finite type $D$-algebras.

source.place: Tag 09IH, lemma-big-extension-is-ok, proof through the dimension calculation; Algebra Tag 00FN

proof.text: Still in case (b), $E=G[1/\pi]$ is Noetherian by localization. It is reduced and every prime is maximal by step 4, hence also minimal. Apply the reduced Noetherian total-fraction-ring decomposition to $E$. Every nonzerodivisor is a unit: otherwise it belongs to some maximal ideal, which is minimal, whereas the cited decomposition says nonzerodivisors avoid all minimal primes. Thus $Q(E)=E$, so the cited isomorphism gives a nonempty finite product $E=\prod_i F_i$ of fields, all algebraic over $L$ by step 4. Under localization, these factors correspond to the minimal primes $\mathfrak a_i$ of $D$. Indeed all minimal primes avoid the nonzerodivisor $\pi$; primes surviving inversion of $\pi$ contract to zero in $B$, and integral incomparability says any two comparable such primes are equal. Localizing $D/\mathfrak a_i$ at $\pi$ is therefore exactly the factor field $F_i$, which is its fraction field.

source.place: Tag 09IH, lemma-big-extension-is-ok, minimal-prime decomposition; Algebra Tag 02LX

proof.text: For each $i$ in case (b), put $T_i=D/\mathfrak a_i\subset F_i$. The contraction of $\mathfrak a_i$ to $B$ is zero: it avoids $\pi$, and every nonzero prime of the DVR $B$ contains $\pi$. Thus $B\hookrightarrow T_i$ is integral. Integral dimension invariance gives $\dim T_i=1$. It is Noetherian by step 6 and semilocal because its maximal ideals are maximal ideals of $D$ containing $\mathfrak a_i$. Apply semilocal dimension-one normalization to $T_i$ in its own fraction field $F_i$. Its normalization $C_i$ is a semilocal Dedekind domain. It is also the integral closure of $B$ in $F_i$: an element integral over $B$ is integral over $T_i$, and the converse follows from transitivity of integral maps. The coordinatewise monic-polynomial argument of step 5 gives $C=\prod_i C_i$. Finite products of Noetherian rings are Noetherian, since their ideals are products of the component ideals; maximal ideals of a finite product come from one factor. Consequently $C$ is Noetherian and semilocal with normal domain factors of dimension one.

source.place: Tag 09IH, lemma-big-extension-is-ok, proof of Noetherianity of the component normalizations; Algebra Tag 09IG with identity field extension

proof.text: The image of $R$ in $E$ lies in $C$, because its elements are integral over $A$, hence over $B$. This gives the required $R\to C$ and the map $D\to C$. The latter is integral, since every element of $C$ already satisfies a monic equation over $B$. Its kernel is the nilradical: the map $D\to E$ has precisely that kernel by step 3, and $C\subset E$. Therefore $G\hookrightarrow C$ is integral and injective. Lying over makes $\operatorname{Spec}C\to\operatorname{Spec}G=\operatorname{Spec}D$ surjective. Faithful flatness of $R\to D$ makes $\operatorname{Spec}D\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ surjective as well. For any maximal $n$ of $R$, select a prime $\mathfrak d$ of $D$ over $n$, then a prime $q$ of $C$ over $\mathfrak d$. Since $\pi\in n$, $\mathfrak d$ contains $\pi$ and is maximal (integrality over $B$); integrality of $D\to C$ then makes $q$ maximal. Thus every maximal ideal of $R$ is attained.

Conversely, for a maximal ideal $q$ of $C$, integrality over $B$ shows $q\cap B=\mathfrak m_B$. Hence $\pi\in q$ and $n=q\cap R$ is a prime containing $\pi$, therefore maximal by integrality of $R/A$. Step 1 makes $R$ a Dedekind domain, and steps 5 or 8 make the factor of $C$ selected by $q$ a Dedekind domain. The Dedekind-localization theorem gives the DVRs $R_n$ and $C_q$; localizing a product at a prime of one factor kills all the other factors. The homomorphism $R_n\to C_q$ is defined by $r/s\mapsto r/s$, since $s\notin n$ implies its image is outside $q$. Its maximal ideal contracts to $nR_n$, so it is local.

In case (a), apply the finite-extension Dedekind theorem to $A\subset R$ and to each $B\subset C_i$ of step 5. It states that all residue field extensions are finite. Since $n$ and $q$ contract to the maximal ideals of $A$ and $B$, respectively, these are exactly the two finite extensions asserted in (a). This application uses no separability hypothesis.

In case (b), let $q_i$ be the maximal ideal in the factor $C_i$ selected by $q$ and let $\mathfrak d_i=q_i\cap T_i$. It is maximal by integrality; $T_{i,\mathfrak d_i}$ is a Noetherian local domain of dimension one, since $T_i$ is a one-dimensional domain and $\mathfrak d_i\ne0$ (it contains $\pi$). The inclusion $T_{i,\mathfrak d_i}\hookrightarrow (C_i)_{q_i}$ has the same fraction field $F_i$ on both sides. The dimension-one finite-residue theorem, applied with extension degree one, gives $\kappa(q_i)/\kappa(\mathfrak d_i)$ finite. The prime $\mathfrak d_i$ lifts to a prime of $U\otimes_A R$; quotienting by $\mathfrak a_i$ and localizing do not change its residue field, so the finite-type residue theorem for $R\to U\otimes_A R$ gives $\kappa(\mathfrak d_i)/\kappa(n)$ finitely generated. Adjoin these finitely many field generators and then a finite basis of $\kappa(q_i)$ over the intermediate field: their union generates $\kappa(q)=\kappa(q_i)$ over $\kappa(n)$. This proves the residue assertion of (b).
